core.title: Serve HTTP with the runtime's native server, not a compatibility framework
core.given: non-test application source, in any layer, of a full-stack application on the profile's runtime
core.when: the application HTTP server, or a route, handler or middleware is added or modified
core.then: Serve HTTP through the runtime's native server construct; construct no HTTP server from a compatibility framework or the platform-compat server API.
prefer: Framework middleware behavior as ordinary function composition around the native server's handlers

During GREEN: add only the route, handler or middleware composition the current acceptance requires; reuse the existing native server instance and routing pattern; when replacing a compatibility server in new work, migrate only the path required for correct behavior
Where the stack provides a streaming HTML transformer reachable only through the native server, assemble and post-process markup fragments there
avoid: Introducing a compatibility HTTP framework or the platform-compat server API for convenience
A compatibility abstraction over a forbidden server
Serving even one route via a compatibility framework: its middleware ecosystem follows and the migration silently stops halfway
unless: Test files: a throwaway test server is not an application server

A name-match of a forbidden server construction that is not an HTTP server (test double, unrelated factory): a known imprecision of the name-based check; rename it (the realization has no per-rule scope)
core.why: Not taste; load-bearing for the stack decision: running a compatibility server keeps the compatibility framework's middleware dependency surface, forfeits the native server capabilities that motivated choosing this runtime, and breaks the selected stack's deployment contract — silently, because the compatibility layer works: the app runs, the tests pass, and the stack has quietly drifted onto the compatibility platform instead of the chosen one. Which capabilities and which deployment properties are at stake is a fact of the selected stack, not of this core.
evidence: The current behavioral acceptance passes through the real native server
The application server remains the runtime's native server construct
The stack's server check reports no forbidden-server finding on non-test source
verification: The check flags, in non-test source, any construction of one of the profile's forbidden server constructions — anything that puts a compatibility HTTP server in front of the app.
The check scans source with string and comment contents masked, so a framework name appearing only inside a string literal or comment (a migration note, an error message) is never flagged.
Test files are out of the check's scope; a throwaway server inside a test file is not scanned.

The match is name-based and known to be imprecise for non-HTTP uses of a forbidden construction's name (test doubles, unrelated factories); the remedy is renaming the match — the realization offers no per-rule scope.

fires: Adding or modifying an HTTP route, handler or middleware in a full-stack application on the profile's runtime
Changing the existing native server (options, routing, connection upgrade, streaming)
Any non-test source file, in any layer, constructs one of the profile's forbidden server constructions
Migrating an existing compatibility-framework route to the native server as part of new work
doesNotFire: A throwaway server spun up inside a test file
A framework name appearing only inside a string literal or comment (e.g. a migration note or error message)
Outgoing HTTP client calls (governed by a separate convention)
Projects that are not a full-stack application on the profile's runtime

profileRequirements.meaning: The languages of production source whose files this rule governs; the realization uses them to recognize its own source files.
The runtime's native HTTP server construct that the application server must be built on (the core's 'the runtime's native server construct').
Construction expressions of compatibility/foreign HTTP servers that must not be constructed in non-test application source (the core's 'the profile's forbidden server constructions').
profileRequirements.bunValue: express(), fastify(, new Koa(, http.createServer(, https.createServer(, bare createServer(

bunOnly.text: 'full-stack Bun application' — the scope is the Bun stack; the workspace gate is the atdd.workspace.bun family implementation.
bunOnly.reason: Stack and workspace identity have no stack-neutral equivalent; the core says 'a full-stack application on the profile's runtime' and the profile's applicability supplies the rest.

bunOnly.text: 'Serve HTTP with Bun.serve; construct no Express, Fastify, Koa or node:http/node:https createServer server.'
bunOnly.reason: The concrete native construct and the concrete forbidden names are carried by the profile keys idiom.module_boundaries#native_server_construct and idiom.module_boundaries#forbidden_server_constructions; the API names themselves are Bun-specific.

bunOnly.text: Exclusive capability premise: 'only Bun.serve has native routing, WebSocket upgrade, streaming and HTMLRewriter (a streaming HTML transformer available only through the Bun server, used for htmx fragments)'. Deployment rationale: running the server directly with the runtime's own command ('bun run server.ts'), no bundle step, no node_modules at runtime. Compat-layer characterization: the stack has quietly become "Node with a faster interpreter".
bunOnly.reason: These premises are facts of the Bun stack, not of every runtime: a native server on another runtime need not provide these particular capabilities, nor a bundle-free, dependency-free deployment. The core's why therefore argues only generically (forfeiting the native capabilities that motivated choosing the runtime, breaking the selected stack's deployment contract) and asserts neither the capability list nor the deployment properties.

bunOnly.text: Assemble and post-process htmx fragments with HTMLRewriter in the Bun server.
bunOnly.reason: HTMLRewriter exists only through the Bun server and htmx is this stack's markup approach; the core keeps only the conditional neutral kernel ('a streaming HTML transformer reachable only through the native server').

bunOnly.text: bun_fullstack_detector reports no foreign_server finding on non-test source.
bunOnly.reason: Detector and finding ids of this one rule are realization details; the core names the check generically.

bunOnly.text: foreign_server patterns: `express()`, `fastify(`, `new Koa(`, `http.createServer(`, `https.createServer(` or a bare `createServer(`.
bunOnly.reason: The exact pattern list is the profile's forbidden_server_constructions value and the Bun detector's match set; the core states the check generically.

bunOnly.text: node_compat_path: Bun's Node.js compatibility layer. It works, which is exactly why this drift is silent: the app runs, the tests pass, and the stack has quietly become "Node with a faster interpreter".
bunOnly.reason: Bun's compat layer has no neutral name; its neutral kernel (the compat layer works, so the drift is silent) lives in the core's why without asserting Bun's specific capability or deployment premises.

bunOnly.text: fact 'language', values [typescript, javascript], note 'Source of a full-stack Bun application (atdd.workspace.bun).'
bunOnly.reason: The closed activation-fact vocabulary has no language fact; the languages are carried as tooling.languages profile data, and the atdd.workspace.bun workspace gate is realization-owned.
Detector and finding ids are realization details; the core keeps a neutral finding kind (forbidden_server_construction).

bunOnly.text: Stack-specific task terms: express, fastify, koa, createServer, Bun.serve.
bunOnly.reason: These terms name specific stacks and APIs; the core keeps only the neutral terms (http server, route, handler, middleware).

neutralityNotes: The core generalizes 'Bun.serve' to 'the runtime's native server construct' and the Express/Fastify/Koa/node:http pattern list to 'the profile's forbidden server constructions'; both need new idiom keys (proposed: idiom.module_boundaries#native_server_construct, idiom.module_boundaries#forbidden_server_constructions) because the closed vocabulary has none. The closed activation-fact vocabulary has no language fact, so the Bun language fact is carried as tooling.languages profile data and the 'atdd.workspace.bun' workspace gate stays realization-owned (bunOnly). core.why deliberately does not assert the specific native capabilities (routing, connection upgrade, streaming, streaming HTML transformation) or the no-bundle / no-installed-runtime-dependencies deployment story: those premises hold for the Bun realization but not for every runtime, so they are recorded only in bunOnly; the core says only that a compatibility server keeps the middleware dependency surface, forfeits the native capabilities that motivated choosing the runtime, and breaks the selected stack's deployment contract, silently because the compatibility layer works. Detector, validator and finding ids are realization-owned; the core's verification names the check generically and keeps the masking, test-file exclusion, name-match imprecision and strict-disposition facts, which are stack-neutral. The htmx/HTMLRewriter prefer example keeps only a conditional neutral kernel; the concrete example lives in the Bun reference. No obligation was dropped or added: both unless items, the masking and client-call non-firings, and the one serve-natively/construct-nothing-else obligation are preserved.
